authors: Kinnaird, E., Stewart, C., & Tchanturia, K.
title: Investigating alexithymia in autism: A systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Across 15 studies, about half of autistic participants (around 50%) had high alexithymia compared with about 5% of comparison participants; alexithymia is common in autism but not universal.
strength: moderate: consistent across studies, but based mostly on self-report questionnaires.
note: Same work as in refs-c; repeated here only to add where it now shows up (Part One, Now: the new section on feelings that are hard to name, bookfixB1).

title: The prevalence of "alexithymic" characteristics in psychosomatic patients
finding: Introduced the term "alexithymia" for difficulty finding words for feelings, along with a limited fantasy life, and found these traits more often in psychosomatic patients than in controls.
strength: early: small clinical sample; historically important as the origin of the term.
note: Same work as in refs-c; repeated here only to add where it now shows up (Part One, Now, bookfixB1).

authors: Crompton, C. J., Ropar, D., Evans-Williams, C. V. M., Flynn, E. G., & Fletcher-Watson, S.
title: Autistic peer-to-peer information transfer is highly effective
finding: In "diffusion chains" where a story was passed along eight people (72 adults), all-autistic chains passed on as much detail as all-non-autistic chains, while mixed chains lost detail faster and reported lower rapport.
strength: moderate: a careful experiment that supports the double empathy idea; modest sample and a single task.
note: Same work as in refs-c; repeated here only to add where it now shows up (Part One, Now: the new double empathy section, bookfixB1).

title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
finding: A large team re-ran 100 published psychology studies with the original materials where they could. 97% of the originals had reported a clear result, but only about a third (36%) of the repeats did, and the effects in the repeats were on average about half the size of the originals.
strength: strong: a large, preregistered, many-lab project; it shows how often single studies fail to repeat, though how to judge a 'successful' repeat is still debated.
note: Cited in the book's 'Reading research' box at the start of the research notes (tools/book/back-reading-research.html, bookfixB1).
